script.title: The Emperor Who Pawned His Palace
script.hook: In 165 AD, a mysterious plague decimated Rome. One third of the population perished. But Marcus Aurelius did something unthinkable.

scenes.narration: In 165 AD, a mysterious plague decimated Rome. One third of the population perished. But Marcus Aurelius did something unthinkable.
scenes.visualPrompt: Marcus Aurelius standing in a candlelit imperial chamber, looking over a stricken ancient Rome through heavy rain.
scenes.soundCue: Distant storm rumbling, mournful cello melody

scenes.narration: Instead of raising taxes on grieving families, he carried the imperial jewels, silk garments, and golden goblets directly into the Forum—and auctioned them to the public.
scenes.visualPrompt: Close up of imperial golden chalices and royal robes placed on auction tables in Trajan's Forum before Roman citizens.

scenes.narration: He wrote in his journal: "Be like the promontory against which the waves continually break, but it stands firm and tames the fury of the water."
scenes.visualPrompt: Craggy sea cliff enduring colossal ocean waves, morphing into marble bust of Marcus Aurelius with warm backlight.

scenes.narration: True power isn't controlling the storm. It’s controlling yourself while the storm rages.
scenes.visualPrompt: Silhouette of Marcus on horseback at dusk on the frontier line, looking forward with stoic resolve.

script.callToAction: Follow for daily timeless wisdom from history's greatest minds.

claims.claimText: The Antonine Plague struck the Roman Empire beginning around 165 AD and caused massive mortality.
claims.evidence: Documented by Galen and contemporary Roman historians; identified generally as an outbreak of smallpox or measles.
claims.reviewerNotes: Independently verified by senior historical researcher against Galen Methodus Medendi.

claims.claimText: Marcus Aurelius auctioned imperial palace furnishings and royal treasures in the Forum to fund the war effort and state relief.
claims.evidence: Historia Augusta (Life of Marcus Aurelius 17.4-5) records a two-month auction in the Forum of Trajan selling gold cups, crystal vessels, and empress robes.
sourceReferences: Historia Augusta, Vita Marci Antonini Philosophi, 17.4-5

claims.claimText: Marcus Aurelius wrote the promontory quote in Meditations.
claims.evidence: Meditations Book 4, Chapter 49: "Be like the cliff against which the waves continually break..."

projects.title: The Real Warning of Icarus: The Sun Was Only Half the Story
projects.description: Daedalus warned his son against flying too high near the sun, but also against flying too low near the sea spray.

ideas.title: The Forgotten Warning: Don’t Fly Too Low
ideas.hook: Everyone remembers Icarus flew too close to the sun. Almost everyone forgets his father's second warning.
ideas.angle: The balance between ambition and apathy
ideas.synopsis: Daedalus warned that the damp sea spray would weigh down the feathers just as fatally as the sun would melt the wax.

script.title: The Real Warning of Icarus
script.hook: You’ve been told the story of Icarus all wrong. Everyone says it's a story about hubris—flying too high. But that was only half the lesson.

scenes.narration: You’ve been told the story of Icarus all wrong. Everyone remembers flying too close to the sun. But that was only half the lesson.
scenes.visualPrompt: Wings made of feathers and beeswax flapping against brilliant azure skies above the Aegean Sea.

scenes.narration: Before strapping on the wings, Daedalus gave two rules: If you fly too high, the heat will melt the wax. But if you fly too low, the ocean mist will soak your feathers and drag you under.
scenes.visualPrompt: Daedalus solemnly binding harness to young Icarus in the stone tower of the Cretan labyrinth.

scenes.narration: The Greeks didn’t just fear overconfidence. They feared complacency. Flying too low is just as fatal as flying too high.
scenes.visualPrompt: Dramatic split-screen: scorching sun on one side, churning dark ocean waves on the other.

script.callToAction: Which danger do you struggle with more: aiming too high, or settling too low? Tell us in the comments.

claims.claimText: Ovid's Metamorphoses records Daedalus warning Icarus against both flying too high and flying too low.
claims.evidence: Ovid, Metamorphoses Book VIII, lines 203-208: "Fly a middle course: if too low, the wave will weight your feathers; if too high, the fires will scorch them."
